mistakes.title: The Scenario field describes a different task
mistakes.dim: Rejected at QC before the rubric is read
mistakes.what: The Scenario on file is not the task you built. Everything downstream — prompts, Draft History, milestones, criteria, golden — is one scenario, and the Scenario field is another, often with a Required Output line naming a deliverable the task never produces.
mistakes.why: Scenario, category and universe are assigned parameters. You cannot change them, and a task that drifts from any of them is rejected however well it is written. When only the field is stale the task is fine, but nobody downstream can tell which of the two is real, so the reviewer has to escalate instead of scoring. When the drift is genuine it is fatal.
mistakes.spot: Open the Story Draft step and read the Scenario field out loud against prompt 1. If the person, the deliverable or the Required Output line do not match, you have it.
mistakes.fix: Read the Scenario back before you write prompt 1, and again as the last check before you submit. Where the two disagree, stop and settle which one is right — never ship both.
mistakes.rule: The scenario, the category and the universe are assigned parameters. The prompt must not drift away from the assigned task parameters, and a build that does is rejected before the rubric is read.

mistakes.title: The deliverable sits below the complexity bar
mistakes.what: The task ships a styled static page — no script, no control, no state, no linked views — while the Agent Objective calls it a dashboard. The scenario and the data behind it are usually strong. Nothing in any prompt asks for interaction, so the page comes out a document.
mistakes.why: The bar is explicit that a styled static page is not interactive HTML, and that a dashboard needs several linked views over data the model extracted itself. A document is the lowest priority deliverable on the table, so the task scores below where the client wants it however good the reasoning underneath is. It is a scenario-stage decision, so it cannot be patched later.
mistakes.spot: Read your own prompts and ask what the page does when someone clicks it. If the answer is nothing, you built a document. The word dashboard in the Agent Objective does not change that.
mistakes.fix: Pick the deliverable type before prompt 1 and check it against the bar's floor for that type. If the data the agent will gather would support a sort, a filter or two linked views, write the prompt that asks for them.
mistakes.rule: “Raising the complexity standard from Blue Shell has been one of the clearest and most consistent client requirements.” Interactive HTML needs “interaction that actually works: controls that respond, state that changes, filters or navigation. A styled static page does not qualify.” A dashboard needs “several linked views over data the model extracted itself. One chart is not a dashboard.” Both are P0.

mistakes.title: The rules point at records the universe does not hold
mistakes.what: The scenario's rules read off a catalog, a policy page, a price list or a subscription that the assigned universe does not contain. Nothing in the folder shows it — the prompts, the rules file and the criteria all read as though the data is there.
mistakes.why: A rule pointing at data no tool returns cannot be followed by any run, so every criterion downstream of it is unreachable. Not wrong — impossible. It takes the difficulty with it too: where the second system is what made the task multi-system, the task ships with one side of every decision resolving to nothing.
mistakes.spot: The tell is in your own golden: a search that comes back empty, a steering turn telling the agent to reach the page another way, and a deliverable that flags its own figures as unconfirmed.
mistakes.fix: At scenario-design time, open the universe and confirm it returns every record your rules point at, one query per rule. An empty search on the first golden turn is a signal to fix the source, never something to steer around.
mistakes.rule: Every requirement the task states has to be reachable with the tools and records the assigned universe actually exposes. A rule pointing at data no tool returns cannot be satisfied by any run, so the criteria resting on it are unreachable rather than hard.

mistakes.title: A steering turn that hands over the answer
mistakes.what: A user turn goes past saying something is wrong and supplies what the agent was meant to derive: the exact file to open, the value, the structure of the answer, or the conclusion. It usually appears after two or three softer turns failed to move the run.
mistakes.why: The steering turns are not graded, but what they produce is. A criterion satisfied by following an instruction no longer separates a strong model from a weak one. It is also how wrong answers get into a rubric: a turn that dictates can dictate incorrectly, and the criteria then get written to match it. The same applies to a turn that settles a question one of your negatives exists to catch — nothing states a value, and the negative can still never fire.
mistakes.spot: Read each of your turns and ask what is left for the agent to work out. Then read your negative criteria against the same turns and check each one is still reachable.
mistakes.fix: Write every steering turn in the voice of the person in the scenario. Say something looks wrong and point at the area — never at the file, the value, the structure or the conclusion. If the model still cannot get there, the scenario needs fixing, not the hint.
mistakes.rule: You are the user, not a second author. A follow up may say something looks wrong and point at the area; it may not supply the file, the value, the structure or the conclusion. Pointing directly at the failure “compromises the 50% failure threshold every task has to meet”, and any leak of a graded value fails the dimension however late in the conversation it happens.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §3 · spec · Multi-Turn - Simulator Answer Leak

mistakes.title: A prompt that answers its own attachment
mistakes.what: A user prompt releases a file and states the value the file exists to make the agent read: how many items are in the photograph, what the total comes to, which of two documents is current. It sits in the same sentence that hands over the asset, written as helpful context by someone who has already looked at the file.
mistakes.why: The no-leak rule covers every turn you write as the user, and it treats a count as a value — the spec's own failing example is “there are five receipts”. Once the value is in the prompt the attachment is decoration: no criterion that depends on reading it can separate a run that opened the file from one that did not.
mistakes.spot: Read each prompt beside the file it releases. Every number, name or conclusion that the file itself carries is a leak, however conversational it sounds.
mistakes.fix: State the requirement — the plates lie flat, the figure has to be the current one — and leave the value to the attachment.
mistakes.rule: A prompt “states the policy directly, removing the work you intended to grade” the moment it carries what the attachment was there to make the agent read. The rule covers every turn you write as the user, and it treats a count as a value.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §3 · spec · Multi-Turn - Simulator Answer Leak

mistakes.title: A deferred asset that announces its own turn
mistakes.what: Material available at turn 1 tells the agent what a later turn will ask. Two shapes: a deferred file named for the turn it belongs to, and a turn-1 document carrying the instruction prompt 2 or 3 was meant to deliver.
mistakes.why: A deferred asset exists to test whether a model can absorb new evidence without a briefing. Told in advance that a file is coming and what to do when it arrives, the model can prepare, and the turn stops measuring anything. Where the advance notice carries the actual instruction rather than a hint of one, the dimension fails outright.
mistakes.spot: Read every turn-1 input as the agent will. If it tells you what a later turn wants, or what to do when a file arrives, you have it. Then read the deferred filenames cold: price_sheet_for_turn3.pdf fails, sheet_02.pdf is fine.
mistakes.fix: Cut the forward-looking sentence out of the turn-1 material and put it in the prompt that delivers the file. Name deferred files for what they contain, not for the turn they belong to. And name the file in the sentence that hands it over, so the turn reads like a person attaching a specific document.
mistakes.rule: deferred_asset is for “material the opening turn did not put in scope”. “The file ships only with the later turn where it enters scope, never with the original task attachments.” Nothing in scope at turn 1 may disclose what a later turn will ask for.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §6.3 · spec · Input Artifacts - Deferred Asset Handling

rows.text:
I took a call yesterday afternoon from Corwin Steadman offering me the Regional Operations Manager position for the Southeast region at $104,000 base, compared to my current $82,000 base as Operations Manager at HAT2. I jotted down the offer details, the travel expectations, and our current wedding and house savings balances on a notepad (see IMG_4412_call_notes.jpg). The promotion starts late summer, which sits about nine months out from my wedding to Adaeze in May 2027. We know our wedding savings are currently tracking behind our committed costs, and we recently had to throttle our monthly house savings to keep wedding expenses cash-funded.

I need an interactive HTML dashboard named dashboard.html that lays out an honest financial comparison between staying at HAT2 versus taking this regional role. Specifically, the dashboard needs to calculate our net take-home cash under both positions after standard income taxes and payroll deductions, project the trajectory of both our wedding fund and house savings fund through our wedding date under both salary tracks, and evaluate how quickly the salary delta would close the wedding funding gap and restore our house savings rate. Please structure this with clear visual KPI cards comparing the gross and net figures alongside a month-by-month trajectory table or chart for both funds through May 2027.

I dug up Jaylen's school calendar for this year and marked it up (see attached IMG_0814_calendar.jpg). My carline mornings are highlighted on it and the custody handovers with Terrance are circled, with the Poplarville details in the margin. Since the regional job runs 60% to 70% travel, about three days a week across the five sites, update dashboard.html with a schedule conflict calendar and a week-by-week matrix across the school year. Map the travel load against what is marked on that calendar, and tell me exactly how many school mornings and how many handovers end up with a travel collision.

Corwin sent over the Southeast region's Q3 travel directives (see attached IMG_0819_travel_policy.jpg). Read it and apply what it actually requires, because it is stricter than what you have modelled and it changes the math. On that schedule we would be out about $200 a month for before-school care, $150 a month for the Poplarville handovers, and $180 a month on meals the company will not cover. Update dashboard.html so those costs come off the raise in the cash comparison, and show me the true adjusted monthly delta and what it does to our savings.

One last thing before I make my final decision. I want dashboard.html to include a dedicated strategic summary section titled "The Cost of the No". Based on all the numbers we have worked through, clearly articulate the trade-off of walking away from this promotion versus taking it, and specify the exact operational and financial conditions that would have to be true for a future regional offer in 2028 to be a sensible "Yes".

mistakes.title: Modifier and Assets Delivered that do not match the turn
mistakes.what: The two fields beside the intent line do not describe what the milestone covers: deferred_asset or revision on an opening turn, none used as a modifier, the agent's own deliverable listed as a delivered asset, or a bare extension where a filename belongs.
mistakes.why: The simulator reads the modifier to decide how it drives the turn, and the assets field to know what arrives when. A wrong label changes the conversation the task actually runs: a revision that revises nothing, a deferred file that was attached from the start, an attachment that never reaches the agent because no milestone asked for it. It is two fields and a five minute pass, which is why it is worth making a habit.
mistakes.spot: Sort your milestone table by turn and read only the two fields. Turn 1 is opening unless the agent has genuinely been handed something new. Assets Delivered names input files the user hands over — never the .html the agent is about to write, and never a bare extension.
mistakes.fix: Set each modifier from the turn's effect on delivered work: opening for a new ask, deferred_asset only when a file actually arrives, revision only when delivered work changes. Then fill Assets Delivered from that milestone's own sub-intent with real filenames. A behavioural or informational sub-intent correctly carries none.
mistakes.rule: Modifier is “what this turn does to work that already exists”, one of the four in §6.3 — “not labels for how a prompt sounds”. opening is “the first turn and any later turn that adds a new requirement without touching work already delivered”; revision is “something already delivered changes”. Assets delivered is “files handed over at this turn, or empty”.

mistakes.title: Stopping rules that do not gate the turn
mistakes.what: Two opposite failures of the same field. Either the clauses cover only part of what the turn asked, so the conversation moves on with a requirement never enforced — or they require something the turn has no way to produce, so a correct run is held at that turn forever.
mistakes.why: Continuation criteria are what the simulator advances on. A missing clause means every later turn builds on a hole. An unsatisfiable clause is worse: the run cannot proceed at all, on a condition the user never created.

mistakes.title: A rubric that can only reward, never penalise
mistakes.what: No negative-weight criteria at all, or so few that the traps the scenario was built around go unscored. Every criterion checks something correct is present; nothing checks something wrong is absent, so the traps the scenario was built around cost a run nothing.
mistakes.why: A scenario earns its difficulty from the wrong answers sitting next to the right ones: the superseded quote, the decoy invoice, the figure from a different part of the store. Without negatives the rubric cannot see any of them, so a run that walks into every trap and recovers scores the same as one that never went near a trap. They are also the cheapest criteria to write, because Leg A usually shows you which failure to write about.
mistakes.spot: Count them. Negatives should be about a quarter of the set. Then check the sign is doing what you think: a negative criterion is a failure when it is Present, so if it reads like something a good run does, it is inverted and it will mark down your own golden.
mistakes.fix: After the Leg A run, read its trajectory for the wrong turns it actually took and write a negative for each one worth catching. State the flaw, never the virtue. Do not invent them to reach a number — but a scenario with no writable negatives usually means the traps are not there.
mistakes.rule: “Negatives should usually make up around 25% of the rubric block and should generally stay below 30%.” They exist for “attractive wrong paths the model has to resist”: “the setup makes it tempting → −3, the setup actively invites it → −5”. A negative criterion is a failure when it is Present, so it has to state the flaw, never the virtue.

mistakes.title: A requirement nothing grades, and a criterion nothing asked for
mistakes.what: Coverage fails in both directions. A requirement stated in a prompt that no criterion checks — most often the nothing-else half of an instruction. And a criterion requiring behaviour no turn requested, usually invented while writing the rubric against the golden instead of against the prompt.
mistakes.why: An ungraded requirement means a run can do the wrong thing and still pass the whole set, which is exactly the failure the rubric existed to catch. A criterion nobody asked for does the reverse: it punishes a run for doing what the user actually said. Both are Major when the requirement is critical to the turn, and the second hides, because the golden often passes it by accident.
mistakes.spot: Walk the prompts line by line and write down which criterion owns each requirement. Then walk the criteria and point at the sentence in a turn that asks for each one. Anything with no partner on either pass is a finding.
mistakes.fix: Write each criterion from the prompt, then check it against the golden — never the other way round. Where an instruction has a nothing-else half, write the closure criterion: X consists only of A, B and C.
mistakes.rule: Every requirement a prompt states needs a criterion that owns it, and every criterion needs a sentence in a turn that asks for it. Missing Criteria and Incorrect Criteria are the two halves of the same check, and both count Major when the requirement is critical to the turn.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §5.1 · spec · Rubric Criteria - Overall Rubric Quality

mistakes.title: Weights that do not separate difficulty from lookup
mistakes.what: Weight 5 and weight 1 handed out without regard to how hard the criterion is: a multi-step cross-source derivation at the same weight as a direct file read, the same operation at 5 in one row and 3 in the next, or two weight-5 criteria resting on a single read of one image.
mistakes.why: The scale exists to separate discovery from lookup. When it does not, the final score says nothing about whether the model did the hard part, and a run that nails every lookup while missing every derivation still scores well.
mistakes.spot: Sort your criteria by weight and read them in order. The order should match the effort the task actually demands. Count the axes each one requires — tool or source coordination, reasoning depth, modality, discovery — and read off +5 for three or more, +3 for exactly two, +1 for one or none.
mistakes.fix: Price by the difficulty of the read: multi-source derivations and media-only values at 5, direct lookups at 1. A two-level miss is what the taxonomy treats as Major.
mistakes.rule: Weight reflects how complex a requirement is to task completion, not how important it feels. Count the axes the criterion actually requires — tool or source coordination, reasoning depth, modality, discovery — and price it on that: three or more is +5, exactly two is +3, one or none is +1.

mistakes.title: More trajectory criteria than the Guidelines allow
mistakes.what: More than five criteria whose Evaluation Target is Trajectory. They are usually good criteria — the agent opened the image, it reached the record before applying it, it did not act on the out-of-scope file — and because each reads well alone, the count creeps up unnoticed.
mistakes.why: The Guidelines cap trajectory rubrics at five, minimum zero, and say to focus on the last response. Past that the set stops grading the deliverable and starts grading the route, and the same evidence usually appears twice: once as a trajectory criterion about the read, once as an artifact criterion about the value it produced.
mistakes.spot: Filter the objective block by Evaluation Target and count the Trajectory rows. Over five is the finding, and it is a count you can run in ten seconds.
mistakes.fix: Drop the ones whose value an artifact criterion already states inline. Trimming is not a loss: the artifact criterion already proves the read happened.
mistakes.note: This corrects the previous version of this course, which asked for more trajectory weight without mentioning the cap. The cap arrived with Guidelines v3 on 10 September 2026, so a habit formed before then is now over it.
mistakes.rule: “Trajectory Rubrics: Maximum of 5, minimum 0. Focus on the last response.” And: “They are NOT mandatory.” This is a v3 change, so a habit formed before September is now over the cap.

mistakes.title: A run that does not fail enough of the rubric
mistakes.what: The task is built, the rubric is written, and the Model A run passes most of it. From inside the task nothing looks wrong: the criteria are sound and the run does fail some. What gives it away is the arithmetic.
mistakes.why: Every task has to be hard enough that the Model A trajectory clearly fails at least 50% of the rubric score. That is a hard client requirement, not a target. A run that sails through most of the set is not separating a strong model from a weak one, and the data is worth less.
mistakes.spot: Add up the weight of every criterion your Model A run failed and divide by the total objective weight. rubric_justifications.md records exactly which ones failed, so this is a number you can read off the folder before you submit.

mistakes.rule: “Enough difficulty that the Model A trajectory clearly fails at least 50% of the final rubric score, with failures that materially affect task completion and the user experience.” It is a core client requirement, not a target to aim near.

mistakes.title: A criterion the golden itself fails
mistakes.what: A criterion whose expected value or wording is contradicted by the task's own golden, its records or its prompt: a phrase quoted at a different length from the one the golden renders, identical wording demanded across two artifacts that legitimately paraphrase each other, a fact the message threads refute, or a file cited that is not in the inputs archive.
mistakes.why: The golden has to pass the complete rubric set. A criterion the golden fails is a broken criterion, not a broken golden, so a correct run gets marked Not Present. Each one counts as Major, and two Majors can fail the task on their own. The commonest cause is a rule that lives only in the Desired Outcome: the agent never sees the outcome, so a criterion resting on it fails a run that did exactly what it was told — and catches your own golden too.
mistakes.spot: Grade the golden against every criterion as the last step before submitting. Separately, read the Desired Outcome clause by clause with the prompts beside it and mark every rule no turn asks for.
mistakes.fix: Where the golden and a criterion disagree, decide which reading is right and rewrite the other two sources to match. Every rule found only in the outcome is a choice: add it to a prompt, or take it out of the outcome and out of any criterion resting on it. Check every filename a criterion cites against the inputs archive.
mistakes.rule: The golden is “the ideal response … the reference point for evaluating subjective quality and for the full pairwise comparison”, so it has to pass the complete rubric set. And the agent only ever sees the prompts: “the Draft History is not embedded in the agent by default … never assume a requirement is in place”, which makes “a rubric demanding a heading that appears only in the Desired Outcome” a requirement the model never saw.

mistakes.title: Criteria a correct run cannot pass, or a wrong one can
mistakes.what: Four shapes of the same defect. Pinning an exact figure the source leaves open. Locking one of several defensible answers when nothing states the rule that picks it. Grading which route a value came from when two sources carry it. Scoping to a step or section, then requiring values that live elsewhere. And the mirror image: a criterion so loose that a run carrying the right answer plus the wrong ones still passes.
mistakes.why: The rubric exists to separate a correct run from an incorrect one. A criterion a correct run cannot satisfy marks down the readers who did the work, and it usually catches your own golden, because the golden followed the evidence while the criterion followed your memory. A criterion with no ceiling costs the distractors the task was built around nothing.
mistakes.spot: For every exact value, name the line, frame or field it comes from. For every criterion naming one item as the answer, ask whether the prompt or the inputs state the rule that picks it. For every criterion that names a step or section, go to that exact moment in your golden and confirm the values are visible there. Then read each one back and ask what wrong run still passes.
mistakes.fix: If you cannot name the source, grade the pattern instead of the value. Where several answers are defensible, add the clause that forces the choice or grade the shape of the answer. Where two sources carry a value, grade that it was retrieved, not which door it came through. Where a run with an extra row survives, add the bound: exactly, only, between.
mistakes.rule: A criterion is checked against what a correct run can actually produce. Pin an exact value only where a source states it, and where the records support more than one defensible answer, the prompt or the inputs have to carry the rule that picks one. The mirror rule is that a criterion has to exclude the wrong run as well as admit the right one.

mistakes.title: Category and Evaluation Target filled with the wrong kind of value
mistakes.what: The two classification fields do not say what they are for. Three shapes recur: a category name written into the target field, an Agent Behavior or Tool Use criterion pointed at the artifact, and a subjective criterion tagged Instruction Following.

Agent Behavior and Tool Use grade the trajectory, so a criterion tagged that way against the artifact is graded in the wrong place. In the subjective block Task Completion is the only valid category, because anything the prompt explicitly asked for belongs in the objective block by definition.
mistakes.spot: Filter by target and read the categories beside it. Agent Behavior and Tool Use always sit on Trajectory. Everything graded on the delivered file sits on Final Answer Artifact. Every subjective row is Task Completion.

mistakes.title: Subjective criteria that never name the file
mistakes.what: The block describes page features without saying which artifact carries them: the page, the body, the commitments table, monument cards. Typically one or two criteria at the top name the file and the rest do not.
mistakes.why: On a task shipping one artifact nothing goes wrong, which is why it keeps getting through. The cost lands the moment a task ships two deliverables, or a revision turn produces a second file: the body stops identifying anything and two graders score the same run against different files. It is one clause.
mistakes.spot: Search the deliverable's filename across the subjective block and check every criterion returns a hit.
mistakes.fix: Open each one with “In <filename>,”. That is the entire fix.
mistakes.rule: Self-contained: “a reviewer should be able to rate the criterion using only the criterion itself and its assigned evaluation target, without reopening the prompt, input files, or another rubric”. That includes the filename the property belongs to.

mistakes.title: Too few criteria carrying too much weight
mistakes.what: Two numbers that go wrong together. The block carries more than 30% of total weight, and it holds five or six criteria where the Guidelines expect ten or more. The ones present are usually sound and cluster on one property, most often whether the page reads as finished.
mistakes.why: The cap keeps the score dominated by deterministic checks. Over it, presentation judgments outweigh whether the task was done. Under the count, the block cannot cover a multi-panel deliverable: a nested table, a timeline strip or a set of diagrams goes ungraded, and two runs presenting the same correct figures very differently score the same.
mistakes.spot: Two sums before you submit. Count the rows — ten is the floor, not the target. Then compute the subjective share using absolute values, because negatives push the real figure above the naive one.
mistakes.fix: Walk the deliverable region by region and write one criterion for whichever region has none. If you are over the cap, grow the objective side first with checks the milestones already imply, and only then trim subjective weights. Leave margin rather than landing on 30.0%.
mistakes.rule: “The expected number of subjective rubrics is 10 or more, but do not optimize for the count itself. The goal is a scenario complex enough to naturally justify 10+ meaningful subjective criteria.” And the block is “capped at 30% of total task weight”, so deterministic checks stay dominant.

mistakes.title: Subjective criteria written from the finished page
mistakes.what: A subjective criterion names the exact heading, button label, row label or column title your golden page happens to use, and requires it. The property underneath is usually real and gradeable. The criterion asks for the wording instead of the property, and none of the quoted strings appears in any prompt — it is your own copy, read back off your own build.
mistakes.why: Subjective rubrics grade how the artifact reads: layout, hierarchy, spacing, consistency. A criterion naming one build's text rejects a subset of valid implementations, and a second correct run presenting the same findings under its own wording fails almost the whole block. Where most of the block is written this way, the count alone carries the task past the failing threshold, so rewriting three or four is not enough.
mistakes.spot: Cover the page and read the criterion again. If it only makes sense with your build in front of you, it is naming your text rather than a property.
mistakes.fix: Write each one from the property down. A label the user fixed in a prompt can be required; a label you chose cannot.
mistakes.rule: Subjective criteria name “ONE observable property of the RENDERED artifact”, graded against the golden side by side — layout, legibility, hierarchy, structure, consistency. A property, not the wording one build happened to use.

mistakes.title: The golden states something its own sources contradict
mistakes.what: A figure, a time, a mapping or a placement written into the golden that the photographed page, the log or the message thread underneath it puts somewhere else. Or a sentence of prose inside the golden stating a total the rest of the same page disagrees with, usually true of an earlier draft. The artifact reads well and every graded column around it is right, which is why it survives to submission.
mistakes.why: The golden is the reference every subjective rating and the pairwise comparison are scored against, so a wrong value in it is graded as correct and a run that reads the source properly is marked down. Where a criterion grades the same detail, the contradiction also makes that criterion unpassable.
mistakes.spot: Take every value the golden asserts that no criterion grades and point at the source line it came from. Ungraded values are where this hides, because nothing else in the task checks them. Then search the golden for every sentence containing a total, a count or a recommendation and check it against the tables on the same page.
mistakes.fix: Correct the golden from the source, in every place the value appears — these travel in threes. A paragraph written at turn 1 is the one most likely to be stale at turn 5.
mistakes.rule: “The golden is not a bonus artifact. It serves as the reference point for evaluating subjective quality and for the full pairwise comparison.” Every value it asserts has to be the one its own sources carry, including the values no criterion happens to grade.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §7 · spec · Golden Solution - Artifact Completeness

mistakes.title: A revision that leaves the old wording standing
mistakes.what: The revision turn changes the thing it was asked to change and leaves every sentence, label and comment that depended on it untouched, so the final artifact states the old position and the new one at the same time.
mistakes.why: Revision Turn Handling fails on a regression, and this is the commonest form: the graded value moves, the prose around it does not. A reader meets an artifact arguing with itself, and a grader reading a criterion against the stale half marks a correct run Not Present.
mistakes.spot: After every revision turn, search the artifact for the value, the label and the name that moved, and read each hit in place.
mistakes.fix: A revision is finished when nothing left on the page describes the state before it. Change one thing precisely, then re-read the whole artifact for every sentence that just became false.
mistakes.rule: For a revision turn, “the golden has to show the edit applied to work that already existed: earlier content kept, the change visible, nothing left stale that depended on it. A total that still includes removed rows, or a header still describing the old state, is a regression.”
mistakes.rule_src: gl §6.3 · spec · Multi-Turn - Revision Turn Handling

mistakes.title: The five minute close-out nobody runs
mistakes.dim: Golden Solution - Trajectory Exclusion · Run Selection
mistakes.what: Five mechanical checks, each cheap, each seen repeatedly. The artifacts archive holding files the prompts never asked for — the generator script, working notes, a build log. No preferred run starred when several completed. A file spelled one way in the prompt and another in the archive. Typos and half-finished clauses in the prompts and criteria a grader has to decode. And a golden conversation that stops before the task's last turn.
mistakes.why: Trajectory Exclusion is scored against the artifacts listing: finished artifacts only, named exactly as the prompts name them, nothing describing how the work was produced. A generator script is the clearest case, because its comments usually say which input each answer came from. An unstarred run leaves whoever opens the task next with only a timestamp, and a later run is not automatically the better one. A criterion citing a filename the archive does not contain is ungradeable. And a grader who has to work out what a clause means is making the judgment the clause was supposed to make.
mistakes.spot: Five lists, side by side, in five minutes. Archive contents against the filenames the prompts name. The run picker reading 1/1 and not 0/1. Every filename character for character. The prompts and criteria read straight through as a grader would. User markers in the golden transcript against populated prompts.
mistakes.fix: Remove anything from the archive that is not a named deliverable, then read each delivered document for build instructions meant for you rather than the reader. Star the run your criteria were written against. The prompt's spelling wins — fix the archive to match it.
mistakes.rule: The artifacts archive is the golden payload: finished deliverables only, named exactly as the prompts name them, with nothing describing how the work was produced. The starred run is the one the rubric was written against, and a criterion that cites a filename the archive does not contain cannot be graded at all.
mistakes.rule_src: gl §7 · spec · Golden Solution - Trajectory Exclusion
